title: Four failures
hookLine: the mind fails four ways: false impressions, unsocial acts, false words, letting the body rule (Meditations 11.19)

cards: Mechanics have a short list of the ways an engine goes wrong. Doctors have one for the body.
Right after his nine reminders, Marcus wrote a short list of the ways a mind goes wrong: four of them, each with a sentence to say when you catch it.
It reads like a small diagnostic card, the kind you could tape inside a kitchen cabinet.

teach.h: FOUR WRONG TURNS TO WATCH FOR.
teach.b: First, the frame. There are four wrong turns of the ruling part of the mind, Marcus writes, to watch for constantly, and wipe out when you catch them, saying a line to each. Second, the first two.
One: a thought you don't need. Say: this thought isn't necessary.
The replay of an old argument, a worry you've already dealt with, a fantasy that goes nowhere. Two: something that pulls people apart. Say: this loosens the bonds between people.
A cutting remark, a bit of gossip, a scheme that works for you by working against others.
Third, words. Three: you're about to say something that isn't what you really think. Marcus counts it among the most absurd things there are, to speak not from your own mind.
Flattery, a fake agreement, a performance. Fourth, the body.
Four: the moment you catch yourself reproaching yourself, because the more divine part of you has been beaten and given way to the less honorable, mortal part, the body and its coarse pleasures.
Notice what he calls it: a defeat of the ruling part, not a crime. So, four questions. Is this thought necessary?
Does this act bind people or break them? Do I mean what I'm about to say?
Who's in charge here, my reason or my appetite?
He doesn't ask himself never to fail. He asks himself to catch it, wipe it out, and keep going.

how: Stoic readers sometimes use Marcus's four checks as a quick daily review: needless thoughts, divisive acts, insincere words, and moments when appetite took over.

o: four mistakes Marcus regretted making as emperor
the mind's four wrong turns Marcus watched for
four sins Marcus said the gods would punish

s: Marcus expected never to fail in these four ways
he tells himself to watch for them constantly and wipe them out when he catches them.
one of the four is saying what you don't really think
he counts speaking not from your own mind among the most absurd things.

games.q: you're about to agree with your boss to keep things smooth, though you don't agree. you're Marcus with his list. which failure is it?
o: speaking not from your own mind.
games.why: that's the third: saying what isn't your real thought, which Marcus counts among the most absurd things.

practice: Look back over the last day and find one of the four: a thought that kept looping, a word that pulled people apart, something you said and didn't mean, a moment your appetite ran the show. Don't scold yourself.
Name it with Marcus's line, this isn't necessary, or this loosens the bonds, or this isn't my real mind, and let it go.

wordCard.voice: Four failures. Marcus's short list of the mind's wrong turns: needless thoughts, unsocial acts, words you don't mean, and appetite in charge. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the ruling part, the mind's command center in Stoic thought. all four failures are its wrong turns.

carryVoice: Your line: wipe it out. Four questions fit on one small card. Day six hundred twenty-five, done.
